DATE:         October 13, 2026                                           ITEM: E-5

FROM:         Planning and Engineering Department

SUBJECT: Authorize the General Manager to Execute a Professional Services Agreement
         with Sierra Controls for the SCADA Infrastructure Improvements Project

RECOMMENDATION:
Authorize the General Manager to execute a Professional Services Agreement, in the amount
of $147,598 with Sierra Controls for the SCADA Infrastructure Improvements Project.

DISCUSSION:
It is a best practice for water and wastewater utilities to rely on SCADA (Supervisory Control
and Data Acquisition) systems to operate their water supply, treatment, and distribution and
wastewater collection, pumping, and treatment systems. SCADA systems have advanced
along with the technology and computer industry to now provide real-time remote monitoring,
automatic control of equipment, historize data, and develop regulatory reports for compliance.

There are four major layers to a SCADA system, (1) field instrumentation, (2) RTUs (remote
telemetry units) and PLCs (programmable logic controllers), (3) communication network, and
the (4) Human Machine Interface (HMI).

The first layer is the field instrumentation at water and sewer stations and remote sites that
monitors water and sewer parameters, including tank levels, flow rates, pressure, pump
status, temperature, etc.

The second layer is the remote terminal units (RTU) and programmable logic controllers
(PLC) at remote sites that communicate with the field instruments and, based on the
programming language installed on these devices, it turns it into a specific command. As an
example, a water tank level field instrument senses the level of water in a tank. The PLC has
a program installed on it that monitors this level and, if the level drops and reaches a
predetermined level, it sends a signal through the RTU to request a water pump to be turned
on to fill the tank; as well as when the tank reaches the predetermined fill level, the PLC
sends a signal to the RTU to request the water pump be turned off.

The third layer is the communication network that uses radio and cellular to transmit the data
collected from the remote field instrumentation at the water and sewer sites, which is
analyzed by the PLC and RTU and then sent to the central control computer. The central
control computer also communicates the necessary commands back to the remote sites to
operate the water and sewer stations based on programmed protocols and operator action.



                                                                                           29
ntpud:2026-10-13:ntpud-agenda-packet:617.30:
The fourth layer is the human machine interface software (HMI) and associated computers
and servers. The HMI is the operating software that is seen on the control computers that the
operators use to monitor and control the water and wastewater system.

In the above example, the water tank is issuing a command that it needs to be filled with
water through the PLC and RTU over the communications network to the HMI. The HMI
determines which water pump station is appropriate to fill that specific water tank and sends
the command back over the communication network, to an RTU and PLC at a remote water
pumping station, that then locally sends a signal to the field instrument to turn a water pump
on that will fill the water tank.

The District’s SCADA systems date back to the late 1960s when audible alarms with red
lights locally announced a failure and phone lines communicated these trouble alarms to an
annunciator panel located at Base. The annunciator panel was essentially a wall map with
light bulbs that lit up when a problem was detected at a remote site. There was very little
detail on what that problem was.

Our modern SCADA system now communicates continuously from all remote water and
sewer sites using radio and cellular networks and displays that information on a collection of
40 different operator screens or pages on PCs and terminals using the Factory Automation
Ignition software program, the HMI.

The proposed scope of work for this project is to upgrade the Factory Automation Ignition
HMI software and associated hardware that will improve the District’s cybersecurity
protection, improve the SCADA reliability and access by hosting it on cloud servers instead of
locally hosted on servers, and improve operability because the new software is compatible
with PCs, tablets, and phones. The scope of work includes the necessary hardware
purchases, software licensing, programming, and initial screen development for nine sites
that have already received hardware and programming upgrades. A general scope of work is
provided after this memo. The specific computer hardware components and details from the
Scope of Work have been removed. As the quote details IT security-critical equipment and is
not subject to public disclosure in accordance with California law, it is not attached to this
memorandum but can be made available to District Board members for review on an as
requested basis.

This upgrade will occur over nine months as the hardware improvements are installed and
programming and screen development occurs. This process completes the groundwork for
future expansion and migration of the remaining sites (approximately 31 screens) from the
current Ignition software to the new Ignition software. Therefore, we will run parallel
platforms until all remote water and sewer sites are migrated to the new software. This step
is necessary because the dramatic changes in the software interface will require operator
adjustment and, more importantly, operator feedback on screen design, data display, and
preferences. Once this standard operator screen is developed, the remaining sites can then
be developed quickly and migrated over. The schedule for this is early Fiscal Year 2027/28.

RECOMMENDATION:
That the Board of Directors consider nominating any director serving on a Placer
County Independent Special District Board to serve as an Alternate Voting Member for
LAFCO for the remaining portion of the four-year term (May 2024-2028), and authorize
the Board President to complete the nomination form.

BACKGROUND:
The District is a Placer County Local Area Formation Commission (LAFCO) member. In
1963, the California State Legislature created LAFCO to encourage orderly growth and
development to protect agricultural resources and open space, discourage urban
sprawl, and provide efficient and effective provision of services. Each county in the
state is required to have a LAFCO. These LAFCOs fulfill their legislative mandate
through the consideration, approval, or denial of boundary changes proposed by
individuals or local agencies. LAFCOs do not have the power to initiate boundary
changes on their own, except for proposals involving the dissolution, consolidation, or
merger of special districts or the establishment of subsidiary districts.

Membership in each county's LAFCO is prescribed by law. The
Placer LAFCO Commission contains seven members: Two representatives from the
County Board of Supervisors, two representatives from city councils, two special district
representatives, and one public member. The current membership is outlined below:

County Members
  • Cindy Gustafson
     Supervisor, District 5
  • Anthony DeMattei
     Supervisor, District 3
  • Shanti Landon, Alternate

LAFCO.

month at 4:00 PM in the Placer County Board of Supervisors’ Chambers, located at 175
Fulweiler Avenue, Auburn, CA. Additional information about Placer LAFCo is available
at: https://www.placerlafcoca.gov. While the Commission currently meets monthly, at
our November meeting they will be discussing moving to an every-other-month
schedule for calendar year 2027.

If the Board decides to nominate a Director, it must do so by formal action and, in doing
